latin.306: GAR. Quaeritur quarto. Cur actuale peccatum Adami tanquam capitis imputetur, quae tamen fuit actio transiens; & non imputetur habituale, sive corruptio Adae, quae fuit vitium permanens? Resp. 1. Hoc ab Apostolo petendum, qui in hoc negotio lapsum & inobedientiam actualem proponit, non autem proponit habitum corruptionis ex illa inobedientia consequentem. PLAC. Cur ab Apostolo id peterem, qui illam imputationem quam impugno non docuit? Deinde si nullum Apostolus proponit habitum corruptionis ex illa inobedientia consequentem, non potest ex Apostolo Pighius refelli, nec probari habitualis corruptio.
latin.307: Quod quam sit alienum a doctrina eorum, quorum opera Deus usus est ad reformandam Ecclesiam, nemo in eorum libris non plane hospes non facile perspicit. GAR. 2. Cum in alieni peccati imputatione, non habitus, sed actiones imputentur, sicut patere potest omnia illa exempla percurrenti, quae supra magno numero producta sunt, quid mirum, si etiam in ista causa non habitus, sed actio tantum Adami memoratur? PLAC. Si habitus sunt peccata, si reos faciunt eos in quibus sunt, quid est cur non possint imputari? Certe, non minus quam actualia nostra, imputata sunt vadi nostro, ut pro eorum reatu satisfaceret. Alienorum autem peccatorum si qua facta est imputatio, unde habes separata ab habitualibus imputata fuisse peccata actualia? Et ut id probari posset, tamen peculiaris est ratio habitus corruptionis Adami, qui fuit peccatum naturae, cum eius causa inobedientia actualis fuerit potius peccatum personae; Ille propagatur cum natura, haec non item.
latin.308: GAR. 3. Imputare alicui peccatum alienum, est ipsum eodem loco habere, ac si in propria persona ipsemet peccatum patrasset, aut commisisset. Atqui habitus non patrantur, neque committuntur. Itaque nec imputantur. PLAC. Quid igitur fiet de peccato omissionis? neque enim proprie patratur aut committitur: immo omissio commissionis opponitur. Vides etiam lector hinc sequi peccatum originis habituale seu corruptionem non esse vere peccatum: omne enim vere peccatum imputatur, nisi condonetur: condonare enim est non imputare peccatum.
latin.309: GAR. 4. Ea ratione foedus a Deo cum Adamo conceptum est, ut quamprimum illud violaret, se & suos illo reatu obstringeret. Violavit autem priusquam habitum corruptionis induisset: & fuit illud actuale peccatum natura prius illo habitu. Ideo actio imputata, non imputatus habitus. PLAC. Utinam vir doctus verba retulisset quibus illud foedus fuit conceptum! Nam si ea nescivit, qui scire potuit illud ea ratione fuisse conceptum? Quid est facilius quam sic rationes fingere?
latin.310: Quod si vox quamprimum abfuit ab illis verbis quibus conceptum fuit, cur eam vir doctus de suo inseruit & addidit? Si in concipiendo illo foedere Deus illa voce usus est, unde habet vir doctus eam significatione tam praecisa esse accipiendam, ut excludat habitum ideo, quia si non temporis forte aliquo naturae momento secutus est actuale peccatum? GAR. Si comparatio instituatur actualis inobedientiae Adami, & consecuta corruptionis habitualis, videbimus hanc corruptionem fuisse effectum illius inobedientiae, atque adeo poenam justo Dei judicio illius peccati actualis. Poena vero non imputatur, sed peccatum potius quod est illius poenae causa meritoria. Quid ergo mirum, si illa inobedientia potius imputata est, quam ista corruptio?
latin.311: PLAC. Hic rursus negatur corruptio imputari, esse peccatum, & doctrina tam opposita confessionibus fidei Protestantium inculcatur. Quod autem ait corruptionem esse illius inobedientiae actualis effectum, si effectum accipit significatione paulo laxiore admitti potest? Se habet enim ad illam inobedientiam ut calor ad calefactionem per quam producitur. Quod vero inde deducit, eam esse poenam illius inobedientiae, non consequitur necessario: non enim omne peccati effectum illius poena est. Certe habitus neque bonarum actionum praemia, neque malarum poenae esse proprie solent. Quomodo autem corruptio poena sit, & justo Dei judicio tribui possit, & supra explicatum est, & infra etiam explicabitur. Caeterum quocunque sensu poena dicatur, id non impedit, quin sit peccatum dignum alia poena, ac proinde imputabile.

pass_a.306: Fourth erotema: why charge Adam's passing act as head-sin, and not the lasting habit of his corruption? GAR points to the Apostle, who names the fall and actual disobedience, not the ensuing habit. Placeus: why ask the Apostle for an imputation he never taught? And if he never sets out that consequent habit, you cannot refute Pighius from him or prove habitual corruption from him either.
pass_a.307: That reading sits far from the reformers whose books any non-stranger can check. GAR's second line: foreign-sin imputation recalls acts, not habits—as the piled examples show—so only Adam's act is remembered here. Placeus: if habits are sins that make their bearers guilty, why should they not be charged? Our Surety bore habitual guilt no less than actual. Even granting someone's claim that only actuals of others were charged, Adam's corruption-habit is a nature-sin propagated with the nature, while his actual disobedience was more a person-sin and does not so propagate.
pass_a.308: GAR's third: to impute another's sin is to treat someone as if he himself had done it; habits are not done, so they are not imputed. Placeus asks what then of omission—never 'done' either, but opposed to commission. Push that rule and habitual original corruption would not be true sin at all, since every true sin is imputed unless forgiven, and forgiveness is non-imputation.
pass_a.309: GAR's fourth hangs on a covenant conceived so that as soon as Adam violated it he bound himself and his; he fell before he wore corruption's habit, so the earlier act is charged, not the habit. Placeus wishes the learned man had quoted the covenant's words: if he never knew them, how does he know it was conceived that way? Inventing such reasons is easy.
pass_a.310: If 'quamprimum' was not in the covenant wording, why did the learned man add it? If God did use it, why take it so tightly as to shut out the habit just because actual sin may have been followed by a nature-moment rather than a time-moment? GAR then compares actual disobedience with ensuing habitual corruption: the latter is effect and just penalty of the former; penalty is not imputed—only the meritorious sin—so of course the disobedience is charged rather than the corruption.
pass_a.311: Placeus: this again denies that corruption is sin and is imputable—a line hard against Protestant confessions. Calling corruption an 'effect' of the act may pass in a loose sense (as heat to heating), but it does not follow that every effect is a penalty; habits are not properly rewards or penalties. However you call it penalty, that still leaves it a sin worthy of further penalty—and so imputable. Tip before GAR's fifth erotema (first generative act / Cain–Seth).

306: GAR. It is asked fourth. Why is Adam's actual sin imputed as of the head, which yet was a transient act; and why is the habitual not imputed, or Adam's corruption, which was a permanent vice? Reply 1. This is to be sought from the Apostle, who in this matter sets forth the fall and actual disobedience, but does not set forth the habit of corruption following from that disobedience. PLAC. Why should I seek it from the Apostle, who did not teach that imputation which I attack? Next, if the Apostle sets forth no habit of corruption following from that disobedience, Pighius cannot be refuted from the Apostle, nor can habitual corruption be proved.
307: How foreign that is from the doctrine of those by whose labors God reformed the Church, no one not quite a stranger in their books fails easily to see. GAR. 2. Since in the imputation of another's sin not habits but actions are imputed, as can appear to anyone who runs through all those examples produced above in great number, what wonder if also in this case not a habit but only Adam's act is remembered? PLAC. If habits are sins, if they make those in whom they are guilty, why can they not be imputed? Certainly, no less than our actual sins, they were imputed to our Surety, that He might satisfy for their guilt. And if any imputation of others' sins was made, whence do you have it that actual sins were imputed separated from habitual ones? And even if that could be proved, still there is a peculiar reason in the habit of Adam's corruption, which was a sin of nature, while its cause, actual disobedience, was rather a sin of the person; the former is propagated with nature, the latter not likewise.
308: GAR. 3. To impute another's sin to someone is to hold him in the same place as if in his own person he himself had perpetrated or committed the sin. But habits are neither perpetrated nor committed. Therefore they are not imputed. PLAC. What then will become of the sin of omission? For it is not properly perpetrated or committed: rather omission is opposed to commission. You see also, reader, that from this it follows that the habitual sin of origin, or corruption, is not truly sin: for every true sin is imputed, unless it is forgiven; and to forgive is not to impute sin.
309: GAR. 4. On this account the covenant was conceived by God with Adam: that as soon as he violated it, he would bind himself and his with that guilt. But he violated it before he had put on the habit of corruption; and that actual sin was prior in nature to that habit. Therefore the act was imputed, not the habit. PLAC. Would that the learned man had reported the words in which that covenant was conceived! For if he did not know them, how could he know that it was conceived on that account? What is easier than thus to invent reasons?
310: But if the word 'as soon as' (quamprimum) was absent from those words in which it was conceived, why did the learned man insert and add it of his own? If in conceiving that covenant God used that word, whence does the learned man have it that it is to be taken in so precise a sense as to exclude the habit for this reason—that if not by some moment of time, perhaps by a moment of nature, actual sin was followed? GAR. If a comparison is instituted between Adam's actual disobedience and the ensuing habitual corruption, we shall see that this corruption was an effect of that disobedience, and so a penalty by God's just judgment of that actual sin. But penalty is not imputed; rather the sin which is the meritorious cause of that penalty. What wonder, then, if that disobedience was rather imputed than this corruption?
311: PLAC. Here again it is denied that corruption is imputed, that it is sin, and a doctrine so opposed to the confessions of Protestant faith is driven in. As for his saying that corruption is an effect of that actual disobedience: if he takes effect in a somewhat looser sense, it may be admitted. For it stands to that disobedience as heat to the heating by which it is produced. But what he deduces from that—that it is the penalty of that disobedience—does not necessarily follow: for not every effect of a sin is its penalty. Certainly habits are not properly either rewards of good acts or penalties of bad ones. How corruption is a penalty, and can be ascribed to God's just judgment, has been explained above and will be explained below as well. For the rest, in whatever sense it is called penalty, that does not hinder it from being a sin worthy of another penalty, and therefore imputable.
